recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows the galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1-2403, one of six huge clusters studied by the Hubble Frontier Fields program. The program has two goals, mapping how mass is spread through these clusters and using them as lenses to see deeper into the distant Universe.

A cluster's gravity bends the light of galaxies behind it, magnifying and distorting them. This is gravitational lensing, and the pattern of bent images reveals how much mass the cluster holds, including dark matter that cannot be seen directly.

Researchers used almost 200 images of distant galaxies, bent and magnified by this cluster, together with the depth of Hubble's data. That let them measure the cluster's total mass more precisely than ever before. Each warped background galaxy adds information, and with enough of them the invisible structure of the cluster can be mapped.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue and visible filters plus one in the near-infrared. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Hubble's long exposures reveal faint, distant galaxies far too dim for the eye, and part of the data is near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

explore: The cluster lies in the constellation Eridanus. Its distance is given as a redshift of 0.396, a measure of how much the expanding Universe has stretched its light on the way to us.
